en: Thus have I heard— the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Twenty-second Discourse of the Dīgha Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a Kuru town named Kammāsadhamma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation...”
For the cessation of suffering and grief, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna— namely,
the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating the mind as the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
The summary is finished.
1. Contemplation of the Body.
1.1. The Section on Mindfulness of Breathing in the Contemplation of the Body And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body as the body?
Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully.
Breathing in long, he understands: "I am breathing in long"; breathing out long, he understands: "I am breathing out long.
Breathing in short, he understands: "I am breathing in short"; breathing out short, he understands: "I am breathing out short."
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body. He trains thus:
‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
Just as, monks, a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, understands: ‘I am making a long turn,’ or when making a short turn, understands: ‘I am making a short turn’;”
In the same way, monks, when a monk is breathing in long, he understands:
‘I am breathing in long’; when breathing out long, he understands: ‘I am breathing out long’; when breathing in short, he understands:
‘I am breathing in short’; and when breathing out short, he understands: ‘I am breathing out short.’
He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body’;
he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.’

Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of both arising and passing away.
Or else, mindfulness that "there is a body" is established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and for mindfulness; and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body.
The section on mindfulness of breathing is finished.
1.2. The Section on Postures in the Contemplation of the Body.

Furthermore, monks, when walking, a monk understands: "I am walking"; when standing, he understands: "I am standing"; when sitting, he understands: "I am sitting"; when lying down, he understands: "I am lying down.
Or, in whatever way his body is disposed, he understands it accordingly.

Thus, he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination in the body; or he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in the body; or he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in the body.

Or else, mindfulness that "there is a body" is established in him just to the extent required for bare knowledge and for constant mindfulness; and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.
The section on the modes of conduct is finished.
1.3. The Section on Mindfulness of the Body and Clear Comprehension:
Furthermore, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead... [and so forth].

He acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside; he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating;
he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus, internally...
[as before] ...In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.
The section on full awareness is finished.

1.4. The Section on Mindfulness of the Body by Attention to Repulsiveness Furthermore, monks, a monk reviews this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys;..."
"The heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; the intestines, mesentery, stomach, and excrement;
bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine.
Monks, it is just as if there were a two-mouthed sack full of various kinds of grain, such as rice.
Of rice, beans, peas, sesame seeds, and husked grain. A man with good eyesight, having released it, would examine it:
"This is rice, these are grains, these are beans, these are peas, these are sesame seeds, these are husked grains.
In the same way, monks, a monk contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity.
‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs … down to … urine.
Thus, either internally … [as before] … In this way too,
bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body.
The section on the contemplation of the repulsive is finished.
1.5. The Section on the Contemplation of the Elements in Mindfulness of the Body.
Furthermore, monks, a monk reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, according to its elements:
‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Just as if, monks, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow and divided it into portions, were sitting at a crossroads;
even so, monks, a monk reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, according to its elements:
‘In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Thus, he dwells contemplating the body as a body internally...
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body.
The section on the contemplation of the elements is finished. 1.6.

The Section on the Nine Cemetery Contemplations in Mindfulness of the Body Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground, dead for one day, or dead for two days, or dead for three days, bloated, discolored, and festering.
He applies this very body [as an analogy]:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this condition.
Thus, internally... [and so forth].
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground,
being devoured by crows, or being devoured by hawks, or being devoured by vultures, or being devoured by herons.
Being devoured by dogs, or being devoured by tigers, or being devoured by leopards,
or being devoured by jackals, or being devoured by various kinds of worms—
he applies this very body [to that]:
‘This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this condition.
Thus, internally...
[as before] ...In this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood still attached, bound together by sinews; ...
a skeleton without flesh and blood, smeared with blood, bound together by sinews; ...
a skeleton free from flesh and blood, bound together by sinews; ... [and so on].
Bones devoid of their connections, scattered in all directions and intermediate directions:
here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle-bone, there a shin-bone, here a thigh-bone,
there a hip-bone, here a rib-bone, there a spine-bone, and here a shoulder-bone.
He places the neck bone in one place, the jaw bone in another, the tooth bone in another, and the skull in another.
He then applies this to his own body:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this fate."
Thus he dwells contemplating the body internally...
[as before] ...Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground—bones whitened, resembling the color of a conch shell... [as before] ...
Bones heaped together, three years old...
bones that are rotten and reduced to powder.
He applies this very same comparison to his own body:
‘This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this condition.

Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally.

Or else, he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of both arising and passing away.
Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ is established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and for mindfulness. And he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body.
The section on the nine charnel-ground contemplations is finished.
The fourteen contemplations on the body are finished.
2. Contemplation of Feelings:
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating feelings in feelings?
In this case, monks, when a monk feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling.
When he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a painful feeling.
When he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
When experiencing a worldly pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a worldly pleasant feeling.
When experiencing an unworldly pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing an unworldly pleasant feeling.
When experiencing a worldly painful feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a worldly painful feeling."

When experiencing a worldly painful feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a worldly painful feeling. When experiencing an unworldly painful feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing an unworldly painful feeling.
When experiencing a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
When experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."

Thus, he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, or he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally, or he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating in feelings their nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in feelings their nature of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in feelings their nature of both arising and passing away.

Or else, mindfulness that "there is feeling" is established in him just to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and for constant mindfulness; and he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings.
The contemplation of feelings is finished.
3. Mindfulness of the Mind.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the mind as the mind?
Here, monks, a monk understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust."
He understands a mind free from lust as “a mind free from lust.
He understands a mind with hatred as “a mind with hatred.
He understands a mind free from hatred as “a mind free from hatred.”
He understands a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion.
He understands a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion.
He understands a contracted mind as "a contracted mind."
He understands a distracted mind as "the mind is distracted.
He understands an exalted mind as "the mind is exalted. He understands a non-exalted mind as "the mind is not exalted."
He understands a surpassable mind as “a surpassable mind”;
he understands an unsurpassable mind as “an unsurpassable mind”;
he understands a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind.”
He understands an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind.
He understands a liberated mind as “a liberated mind.
He understands an unliberated mind as “an unliberated mind.”

Thus he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind internally, or he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind externally, or he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind both internally and externally.

Or else he dwells contemplating in the mind its nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in the mind its nature of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in the mind its nature of both arising and passing away.

Or else, mindfulness that “there is mind” is established in him just for the sake of bare knowledge and for the sake of constant mindfulness; and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the mind as mind.
Contemplation of the Mind is finished.
4. Contemplation of Phenomena (Dhammānupassanā) 4.1.
The Section on the Hindrances (Nīvaraṇapabba) And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena?
“Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena with regard to the five hindrances.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena among phenomena with regard to the five hindrances?
Here, monks, if sensual desire is present within him, a monk knows: ‘Sensual desire is present within me.’”
He understands; or, when sensual desire is absent within him, he understands: "There is no sensual desire in me.

He understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen sensual desire, and he understands how there comes to be the future non-arising of abandoned sensual desire.
There is non-arising, and he understands that.
Or, when ill will is present within him, he understands: "There is ill will within me";
or when ill will is not present within him, he understands: "There is no ill will within me. And he understands how unarisen [ill will]...
There is the arising of ill will, and he understands that; he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen ill will;
and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of abandoned ill will in the future.
Or, when sloth and torpor are present within him, he understands: "There is sloth and torpor in me"; when they are not present...
Or, when there is no sloth and torpor within him, he understands: "There is no sloth and torpor within me.
He understands how the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor comes about; he understands how the abandoning of arisen sloth and torpor comes about;
and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned sloth and torpor will come about in the future.
When restlessness and remorse are present within him, he understands: "There is restlessness and remorse within me";
when restlessness and remorse are not present within him, he understands: "There is no restlessness and remorse within me.
He also understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and how...
He understands the abandoning of restlessness and remorse that has arisen, and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of abandoned restlessness and remorse in the future.
Or, when doubt is present within him, he understands: "There is doubt within me"; when it is absent...
Or, when there is doubt within him, he understands: ‘There is no doubt within me.
He understands how the arising of unarisen doubt comes to be; he understands how the abandoning of arisen doubt comes to be;
and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned doubt will come to be in the future.

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena.

Or else, mindfulness that “there are mental phenomena” is established in him just for the sake of bare knowledge and for the sake of constant mindfulness; he dwells independent and does not cling to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating mental phenomena as mental phenomena in regard to the five hindrances.
The section on the hindrances is finished.
4.2. The Section on the Aggregates in the Mindfulness of Phenomena Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena in regard to the five aggregates of clinging.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena among phenomena in regard to the five aggregates of clinging?
"Here, monks, a monk [reflects]: 'Such is form, such its arising, such its passing away;
such is feeling, such its arising, such its passing away.'"
‘Such is perception, such is the arising of perception, such is the passing away of perception;
such are volitional formations, such is the arising of volitional formations, such is the passing away of volitional formations;
such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’”

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena.
Or else, mindfulness that “there are phenomena” is established in him just for the sake of bare knowledge and bare mindfulness; and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the five aggregates of clinging.
The section on the aggregates is finished.

4.3. The Section on the Bases in the Contemplation of Phenomena (Dhammānupassanā-Āyatana-pabba) Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the six internal and external bases.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the six internal and external bases?
"Here, monks, a monk understands the eye, he understands forms, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both;
he understands how there comes to be the arising of an unarisen fetter,
and he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of a fetter once arisen."
And he understands the non-arising in the future of that fetter which has been abandoned.
He understands the ear, he understands sounds, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both;
and he understands how the arising of an unarisen fetter occurs, and he understands that as well.
He understands the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of the abandoned fetter in the future.
He understands the nose, he understands odors, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both.
And he understands that; he understands how there is the arising of an unarisen fetter;
he understands how there is the abandoning of an arisen fetter; and he understands how there is the future non-arising of an abandoned fetter.
He understands the tongue; he understands tastes; he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both;
he understands how there comes to be the arising of an unarisen fetter; he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of a fetter that has arisen;
and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of a fetter that has been abandoned.
There is non-arising in the future, and he understands that.
He understands the body; he understands tangibles; he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both;
and he understands how the arising of an unarisen fetter occurs. And he understands...
He understands the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of the abandoned fetter in the future.
He understands the mind, he understands mental phenomena, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both.
And he understands that; he understands how there is the arising of an unarisen fetter;
he understands how there is the abandoning of a fetter that has arisen; and he understands how there is the non-arising in the future of a fetter that has been abandoned.

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is established in him just for the sake of bare knowledge and for the sake of constant mindfulness; he dwells independent and does not cling to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the six internal and external sense bases.
The section on the sense bases is finished.

4.4. The Section on the Factors of Enlightenment in the Contemplation of Phenomena Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena in regard to the seven factors of enlightenment.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena among phenomena in regard to the seven factors of enlightenment?
In this case, monks, a monk, when the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is present within him, understands: ‘The enlightenment factor of mindfulness is present within me’;
or when the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is not present within him, he understands: ‘The enlightenment factor of mindfulness is not present within me’;
and he understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness comes to arise.

And he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment of the development of the mindfulness enlightenment factor that has arisen; and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment of the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor that has arisen.
Or, when the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is present within him, he understands: "The investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is present within me";
or when the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is not present within him, he understands: "The investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is not present within me."
He understands it; he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-dharmas enlightenment factor;
and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the arisen investigation-of-dharmas enlightenment factor.
Or, when the energy enlightenment factor is present within him, he understands: "The energy enlightenment factor is present within me."
He understands it; or, if the enlightenment factor of energy is not present within him, he understands, ‘The enlightenment factor of energy is not present within me.
He understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy comes to arise, and he understands how the fulfilled development of the enlightenment factor of energy that has arisen comes to be.
When the enlightenment factor of rapture is present within him, he understands: ‘The enlightenment factor of rapture is present within me’;
or when the enlightenment factor of rapture is not present within him, he understands: ‘The enlightenment factor of rapture is not present within me.
He also understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture comes to arise, and how the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture...
There is the fulfillment through the development of the enlightenment factor of rapture, and he understands that.
Or, when the enlightenment factor of tranquility is present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of tranquility is present within me";
or, when the enlightenment factor of tranquility is not present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of tranquility is not present within me."

He understands it; he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment of tranquility, and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
Or, when the factor of enlightenment of concentration is present within him, he understands: "The factor of enlightenment of concentration is present within me."
He understands it; or, when the enlightenment factor of concentration is absent within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of concentration is not present within me.

He understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration comes to arise, and he understands how the cultivation of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration reaches its fulfillment.
When the enlightenment factor of equanimity is present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of equanimity is present within me";
when the enlightenment factor of equanimity is not present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of equanimity is not present within me";
and he also understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity comes to arise.
And he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment of the development of the arisen factor of equanimity-enlightenment.

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating in phenomena the nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in phenomena the nature of vanishing, or he dwells contemplating in phenomena the nature of both arising and vanishing.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is established in him just for the sake of knowledge and for the sake of mindfulness; he dwells independent and does not cling to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the seven factors of enlightenment.
The section on the factors of enlightenment is finished.
4.5. The Section on the Truths in the Contemplation of Phenomena Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena in terms of the Four Noble Truths.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena in terms of the Four Noble Truths?
In this case, monks, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is:
‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’
The first recitation section is finished.
4.5.1. Exposition of the Noble Truth of Suffering:
And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering?
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering;
association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not to obtain what one desires is suffering;
in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
And what, monks, is birth? That which,
for various beings in their respective classes of beings, is birth, being born, descent, manifestation, the appearance of the aggregates, and the acquisition of the sense-bases—
this, monks, is called birth.
And what, monks, is aging? That which,
for various beings in their respective classes of beings, is aging, decrepitude, brokenness, graying of hair, wrinkling of skin, the decline of the life-span, and the maturation of the faculties—
this, monks, is called aging.

And what, monks, is death? That which, for various beings, from their respective classes of beings, is the passing away, the falling away, the breaking up, the disappearance, the mortality, the death, the completion of time, the breaking up of the aggregates,
the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life-faculty— this, monks, is called death.
And what, monks, is sorrow? Whatever sorrow, monks,
there is for one who has encountered some kind of misfortune or is touched by some kind of painful state— sorrowing, the act of sorrowing, the state of being sorrowful,
inner sorrow, inner anguish— this, monks, is called sorrow.
And what, monks, is lamentation? Whatever, monks,

for one who has encountered some kind of misfortune or is touched by some kind of painful state, is wailing, lamenting, the act of wailing, the act of lamenting, the state of having wailed, the state of having lamented—
this, monks, is called lamentation.
And what, monks, is suffering?
Whatever, monks, is bodily pain, bodily unpleasantness, painful feeling arisen from body contact, an unpleasant experience—
this, monks, is called suffering.
And what, monks, is mental grief? That which, monks,
is mental suffering, mental unease, born of mind-contact, painful and unpleasant feeling—
this, monks, is called mental grief.
And what, monks, is despair? Whatever, monks,
is the distress, the despair, the state of being distressed, the state of being despaired of one who is possessed of some particular misfortune or touched by some particular state of suffering—
this, monks, is called despair.
And what, bhikkhus, is association with the unpleasant as suffering?
Here, there are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable to one;
or there are those who wish one no welfare, who wish one harm, who wish one discomfort, and who wish one lack of security from bondage—it is the association with these.
Being together with, meeting with, encountering,
and mingling with them— this, monks, is called association with the unpleasant,
which is suffering. And what, monks, is separation from the pleasant, which is suffering?
In this case, there are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena that are desirable, lovely, and pleasing to one;
or there are those who wish for one's welfare, one's benefit, one's comfort, and one's security from bondage—
such as a mother, father, brother, sister, friend, colleague, or kinsman by blood— and the lack of association with them.
Non-meeting, non-union, and lack of mingling with those who are dear—
this, monks, is called the suffering of separation from the beloved.
And what, monks, is the suffering of not getting what one desires?
“Bhikkhus, for beings subject to birth, such a wish arises:
‘O, that we were not subject to birth! O, that birth would not come upon us!
Yet this is not to be attained by mere wishing.”
This too is suffering: not getting what one wishes for.
For beings subject to aging, monks, this wish arises:
"O, that we were not subject to aging; oh, that aging would not come upon us!"
But this is not to be obtained by wishing; thus, not getting what one wishes for is also suffering.
For beings subject to illness, monks, such a wish arises: "O, that we were not subject to illness! O, that illness would not come upon us!
But this is not to be obtained by wishing; thus, not getting what one wishes for is also suffering.
“Bhikkhus, for beings subject to death, such a wish arises: ‘O, that we were not subject to death! O, that death would not come to us!
Yet this cannot be attained by wishing; thus, not getting what one wishes for is also suffering.
For beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, bhikkhus, such a wish arises:”
‘Oh, that we might not be subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
oh, that sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair might not come upon us!
Yet this cannot be attained by mere wishing.
This too is suffering: not to get what one desires.
And what, bhikkhus, in brief, are the five aggregates subject to clinging that are suffering? They are as follows:

the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
"These, monks, are called, in brief, the five aggregates of clinging as suffering.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering.
4.5.2. Exposition of the Truth of the Origin (Samudayasaccaniddesa)
And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there;
namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Now, monks, where does this craving arise when arising, and where does it settle when settling?
It arises where there is something in the world that is agreeable and pleasurable; it settles where there is something in the world that is agreeable and pleasurable.
And what in the world is agreeable and pleasurable?
The eye is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
The ear in the world … the nose in the world … [and so on].
The tongue in the world...
the body in the world...
the mind in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Forms in the world… sounds in the world… odors in the world…
Tastes in the world...
tangibles in the world...
mental phenomena in the world are lovely and pleasant; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Eye-consciousness in the world… ear-consciousness in the world… nose-consciousness in the world…
Tongue-consciousness in the world...
body-consciousness in the world...
mind-consciousness in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Eye-contact in the world...
ear-contact in the world...
nose-contact in the world...
Tongue-contact in the world...
body-contact in the world...
mind-contact in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
Feeling born of eye-contact in the world...
feeling born of ear-contact in the world...
feeling born of nose-contact in the world...
Feeling born of tongue-contact in the world...
feeling born of body-contact in the world...
feeling born of mind-contact in the world is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Perception of forms in the world … perception of sounds in the world … perception of odors in the world …
In the world, the perception of tastes... the perception of tangibles...
the perception of mental phenomena is a lovely form, a pleasant form; it is here that this craving, when arising, arises, and here, when settling, settles.
Volition regarding forms in the world … volition regarding sounds in the world … volition regarding odors in the world …

Volition regarding tastes in the world… volition regarding tangibles in the world… volition regarding mental phenomena in the world is a form that is dear and pleasant; it is here that this craving, when arising, arises, and here, when settling, settles.
Craving for forms in the world … craving for sounds in the world … craving for odors in the world …
Craving for tastes in the world...
craving for tangibles in the world...
craving for mental phenomena in the world is a form that is dear and pleasant; herein this craving arises when it arises, and herein it settles when it settles.
In the world, there is reflection on forms;
in the world, there is reflection on sounds;
in the world, there is reflection on odors.
In the world, reflection on tastes... reflection on tangibles...
reflection on mental phenomena is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
Discernment of forms in the world… discernment of sounds in the world… discernment of odors in the world…
Discernment of tastes in the world...
discernment of tangibles in the world...
discernment of mental phenomena in the world is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
4.5.3. Exposition of the Truth of Cessation:
And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, its abandonment, its liberation, and the absence of attachment to it.
Now, monks, where is this craving abandoned when it is being abandoned, and where does it cease when it is ceasing?
It is toward whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable that this craving is abandoned when it is being abandoned, and there it ceases when it is ceasing.
And what in the world is lovely and pleasant?

The eye is lovely and pleasant in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases. The ear in the world … [and so on for the nose, tongue, body, and mind] … [and their respective objects] … [and their respective consciousnesses] … [and their respective contact] … [and their respective feeling] … [and their respective perception] … [and their respective volition] … [and their respective craving] … [and their respective clinging] … [and their respective becoming] … [and their respective birth] … [and their respective aging-and-death] … herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases.
The nose in the world...
the tongue in the world...
the body in the world...
The mind is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
Visible forms in the world… sounds in the world…
Odors in the world … tastes in the world … tangibles in the world …
In the world, mental phenomena are dear and pleasant; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, it ceases.
Eye-consciousness in the world...
ear-consciousness in the world...
Olfactory consciousness in the world...
gustatory consciousness in the world...
tactile consciousness in the world...

Mental consciousness is a lovely thing and a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases. Eye-contact is a lovely thing and a pleasant thing in the world… ear-contact is a lovely thing and a pleasant thing in the world…
In the world, nose-contact … tongue-contact … body-contact … [is impermanent].
Mental contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases.
Feeling born of eye-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world...
feeling born of ear-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world...
In the world, feeling born of nose-contact… feeling born of tongue-contact… feeling born of body-contact…
Feeling born of mind-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
Perception of forms in the world… perception of sounds in the world…
Perception of odors in the world… perception of tastes in the world… perception of tangibles in the world…
Perception of mental phenomena is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases.
Volition regarding forms in the world… volition regarding sounds in the world…
In the world, there is volition regarding odors;
in the world, there is volition regarding tastes;
in the world, there is volition regarding tangibles.
Volition regarding mental phenomena (*dhamma*) is a form of endearment and a form of gratification in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases.
Craving for forms in the world… craving for sounds in the world…
Craving for odors in the world...
craving for tastes in the world...
craving for tangibles in the world...
In the world, craving for phenomena consists of what is dear and what is pleasant; it is here that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and here that it, when ceasing, ceases.
In the world, there is thinking about forms… thinking about sounds…
In the world, there is reflection on odors;
in the world, there is reflection on tastes;
in the world, there is reflection on tangibles.
Thought of mental phenomena (*dhamma-vitakka*) is a form that is dear and pleasant in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
Discursive thought regarding forms (*rūpa-vicāra*) in the world… discursive thought regarding sounds (*sadda-vicāra*) in the world…
Investigation of odors in the world...
investigation of tastes in the world...
investigation of tangibles in the world...
Investigation of phenomena is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, while being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, while ceasing, it ceases.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
4.5.4. Exposition of the Truth of the Path:
"And what, monks, is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is this very noble eightfold path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
And what, monks, is right view?

It is, monks, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin of suffering, the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and the knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, monks, is called right view.
And what, monks, is right intention?
The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty.
This, monks, is called right intention.
And what, monks, is right speech?
Refraining from false speech, refraining from malicious speech, refraining from harsh speech, and refraining from idle chatter.
This, monks, is called right speech.
And what, monks, is right action?
Refraining from taking life, refraining from taking what is not given, and refraining from sexual misconduct.
This, monks, is called right action.
And what, monks, is right livelihood?
Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, maintains his life by right livelihood.
This, monks, is called right livelihood.
And what, monks, is right effort?
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;

one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.
This, monks, is called right effort.
And what, monks, is right mindfulness?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
This, monks, is called right mindfulness.
And what, monks, is right concentration?

Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness. Thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This, monks, is called right concentration.
This, monks, is called the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

Thus, one dwells contemplating phenomena among internal phenomena, or one dwells contemplating phenomena among external phenomena, or one dwells contemplating phenomena among both internal and external phenomena.

Or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination in phenomena; or he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in phenomena; or he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in phenomena.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is established in him just to the extent required for bare knowledge and for constant mindfulness; and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the four noble truths.
The Chapter on Truth is finished.
The Contemplation of Phenomena is finished.

Monks, whoever should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years, one of two fruits may be expected for them: either final knowledge here and now, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning.
"Full knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue of clinging, the state of a non-returner.
Let alone seven years, monks;
for whoever, monks, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for six years … [and so on]."
For five years … for four years … for three years …
Two years...
one year...
let alone, monks, one year.
"Monks, whoever should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven months, one of two fruits may be expected for them:
either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner.
Let alone seven months, monks."
"Monks, whoever should develop these four foundations of mindfulness for six months...
five months...
four months..."
For three months … for two months … for one month …
"For half a month...
Let alone half a month, monks.

For whoever, monks, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness thus for even seven days, one of two fruits may be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-return."
"Full knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue of clinging, the state of a non-returner.

"Monks, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say:"
"The four foundations of mindfulness.
Thus it was said; this is in reference to that which was said.
This is what the Blessed One spoke.
The bhikkhus were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.
The Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness is finished; it is the ninth.
